channel.title: Juan, Attorney at Law — Korean Law Guides for Foreign Nationals
channel.description: Plain-English guides to Korean law for foreign residents — immigration and visas, criminal defense, employment, real estate, family law, and tax.

item.title: Changing Your Visa Status Inside Korea: The Status Change Permit (체류자격 변경허가)
item.description: How the status change permit (체류자격 변경허가) differs from an extension, which switches require leaving Korea, and the timing mistake that turns a change into an overstay.

item.title: Hit-and-Run (뺑소니) in Korea: The Penalty Gap Foreign Drivers Never See Coming
item.description: Why driving away turns an ordinary traffic case into a felony under the Aggravated Punishment Act, and why comprehensive insurance does not close it.

item.title: Enrolling a Foreign Child in a Korean Public School: Residence, Not Visa Status
item.description: Enrollment (취학) in a Korean public school runs on proof of residence, not visa status. The documents, the grade placement review, and what to do if a school refuses.

item.title: Damages Without a Second Lawsuit: The Compensation Order (배상명령)
item.description: A crime victim in Korea does not always have to sue twice. The criminal court can order the defendant to pay — but only for certain offences, and only for certain losses.

item.title: Seven Days: Appealing a Criminal Conviction (항소) in Korea
item.description: The verdict is not the end. But the window is seven days, and it starts running the day it is pronounced — not the day the written judgment arrives.

item.title: Acting From Abroad: The Power of Attorney (위임장) in Korea
item.description: A power of attorney that is valid is not the same as one a Korean bank will accept. The difference is usually in the authentication, and in how narrowly it is drafted.

item.title: Investing Your Way In: The D-8 Corporate Investment Visa (기업투자) in Korea
item.description: The money does not buy the visa. A foreign-investment report does, and it has to be filed before the money moves. The order that decides everything.

item.title: Held, Not Charged: Immigration Detention (보호) and Temporary Release (보호일시해제) in Korea
item.description: No charge, no trial, no sentence — and detention that continues while the deportation order is litigated. The routes out, and the one that decides whether you can ever come back.

item.title: The Clause That Follows You Out: Non-Compete (경업금지) and Confidentiality in Korean Employment Contracts
item.description: A non-compete is not void in Korea, and it is not automatically valid either. The six factors, the consideration question, and the injunction that lands before anyone argues the merits.

item.title: The Courtroom Sequence: Standing Trial (공판) in Korea as a Foreign National
item.description: Interpretation covers the hearing, not the case file. The order a Korean hearing follows, a sentence pronounced in about a minute, and the seven days that start running that same day.

item.title: Winning Is Not Collecting: Enforcing a Judgment (강제집행) in Korea
item.description: Attachment of claims (채권압류) reaches a bank account in days; an auction takes months and may yield nothing. Which route fits what you found, and the ten-year clock on the judgment.

item.title: Fifty-Two and Five: Working Hours, Overtime and Annual Leave (연차) in Korea
item.description: Below five employees, a sixty-hour week can be lawful and owe nothing extra. The premiums, the leave that becomes cash on termination, and the clause that tries to absorb both.

item.title: Your Record on Paper: Criminal Record Certificates (범죄경력회보서) in Korea
item.description: A suspended indictment (기소유예) is not a conviction, but it is still on a record — a different one. Which certificate shows what, who is entitled to ask for it, and how long the entries stay there.

item.title: The Agreement That Ends the Case: Settlement (합의) in Korean Criminal Matters
item.description: Paying the victim ends some Korean prosecutions completely and others not at all. Which offences, what the written agreement must contain, the deadline that closes the option, and what to do when the victim will not talk.

item.title: Turned Back at the Border: Entry Refusal (입국불허) at a Korean Airport
item.description: The entry decision belongs to the officer at the port, not to the mission that issued the visa. What secondary inspection actually involves, why the statement you sign matters more than the interview, and the difference between being refused once and being banned.

item.title: When Immigration Says No: Challenging a Korean Immigration Decision
item.description: Refused an extension or served with a departure order? Three routes exist, the clock is 90 days, and filing does not stop removal — which is why suspension of execution (집행정지) matters more than the appeal itself.

item.title: The Deadlines That Decide Your Case: Limitation Periods (시효) in Korea
item.description: Korean law puts a deadline on nearly every claim, and it runs from earlier than you think. The civil, criminal, and labour periods, how interruption actually works, and the rule that matters most to people who leave Korea.

item.title: After the Marriage Ends: Keeping an F-6 Visa (결혼이민) in Korea
item.description: Divorce does not automatically end an F-6 visa — but keeping it means proving the Korean spouse's fault (귀책사유). A Korean attorney explains F-6-3, the route through a child, and the alternatives when fault cannot be shown.

item.title: The Two-Year Rule: Fixed-Term Contracts (기간제) in Korea and the Renewal Nobody Promised You
item.description: Work more than two years on fixed-term contracts (기간제) in Korea and the law can treat you as permanently employed — but the exceptions are wide. A Korean attorney explains the two-year rule, the expectation of renewal (갱신기대권), and what a non-renewal means for your visa.

item.title: Illegal Filming (불법촬영) Charges in Korea: The Phone, the Forensics, and What Counts as a Crime
item.description: Illegal filming (불법촬영) under the Sexual Violence Punishment Act carries up to seven years in prison — and in Korea, possessing or watching the footage is a separate offence. A Korean attorney explains what the law covers, what a phone forensic examination finds, and what follows a foreign national beyond the sentence.

item.title: Freezing the Money First: Provisional Attachment (가압류) in Korea
item.description: Winning a Korean lawsuit against an empty account is worth nothing. Provisional attachment (가압류) freezes a debtor's property before they can move it. A Korean attorney explains what can be frozen, what it costs, and how debtors fight back.

item.title: The D-4 Language Student Visa (어학연수) in Korea: Attendance, Part-Time Work, and the Way Out
item.description: A D-4 visa (어학연수) buys you a language course, not a life in Korea — attendance is monitored, part-time work needs permission you do not have on arrival, and the extension is decided on your record. A Korean attorney explains the conditions, the work permit, and the route to a D-2 student visa.

item.title: Banned From Leaving Korea: The Departure Suspension (출국정지) Nobody Warns You About
item.description: A foreigner under investigation in Korea is not given a departure ban (출국금지) — the measure is a departure suspension (출국정지), and most people discover it at the airport check-in counter. A Korean attorney explains who gets one, how long it lasts, and the two ways to fight it.

item.title: Court Papers in Korean: What to Do When You Are Sued in Korea
item.description: A payment order (지급명령) gives you two weeks. A complaint (소장) gives you thirty days. Ignore either and the court decides without you. A Korean attorney explains the three envelopes a foreign defendant receives, the deadlines attached to each, and what to do if you never got the papers at all.

item.title: Accused of Indecent Act by Force (강제추행) in Korea: What Follows Long After the Sentence
item.description: Indecent act by force (강제추행) is charged far more broadly in Korea than foreigners expect, settlement no longer ends the case, and a conviction brings registration, employment restrictions and immigration consequences. A Korean attorney explains what happens and when counsel matters.

item.title: Applying for Refugee Status (난민) in Korea: The Process, the Deadlines, and the Alternative
item.description: Refugee status (난민) in Korea is decided on an interview, refused far more often than granted, and appealed on deadlines measured in days. A Korean attorney explains the two application routes, what you may do while waiting, and how humanitarian stay (인도적체류허가) differs.

item.title: Sending Money Out of Korea: The Foreign Exchange Rules (외국환거래) Behind a Blocked Transfer
item.description: Korean banks refuse outbound transfers for documentation reasons, not amounts. A Korean attorney explains the foreign exchange rules (외국환거래), what evidence each category of money requires, the rule against split remittances (분할송금), and how to move funds when you leave for good.

item.title: Alien Registration (외국인등록) and Address Reporting in Korea: The Small Duties That Cost People Their Status
item.description: Alien registration (외국인등록) and the 14-day change-of-address report (체류지 변경신고) are the easiest immigration duties to forget and among the most expensive. A Korean attorney explains the deadlines, the fines, and how a missed report surfaces years later at renewal.

item.title: Filing a Criminal Complaint (고소장) in Korea as a Foreigner: How a Victim Actually Starts a Case
item.description: Someone defrauded, assaulted, or threatened you in Korea and you want them prosecuted. A Korean attorney explains the criminal complaint (고소장), what the police do with it, why non-prosecution is common, and the appeal routes a victim has.

item.title: The D-10 Job Seeker Visa (구직) in Korea: The Bridge Status Between One Job and the Next
item.description: The D-10 job seeker visa (구직) buys time to find work in Korea — but it is scored on points, limited in duration, and strict about what you may do while holding it. A Korean attorney explains eligibility, extensions, and the mistakes that end the status early.

item.title: Arrested in Korea: The Detention Warrant Hearing (구속영장실질심사) and How to Get Out
item.description: Police can hold you 48 hours before a judge decides whether you stay. A Korean attorney explains the detention warrant hearing (구속영장실질심사), why foreigners are found to be flight risks, and the two routes out — detention review and bail.

item.title: The F-2-7 Points-Based Residence Visa (거주) in Korea: Scoring, Eligibility, and Why It Beats an Employer-Tied Visa
item.description: The F-2-7 points-based residence visa (거주) frees you from employer sponsorship and shortens the road to permanent residency. A Korean attorney explains how the scoring works, who can apply, and where applications actually fail.

item.title: Getting Married in Korea as a Foreigner: The Marriage Report (혼인신고) That Actually Creates the Marriage
item.description: In Korea the wedding does not marry you — filing the marriage report (혼인신고) does. A Korean attorney explains the documents a foreign spouse needs, what the district office checks, and why the marriage and the F-6 visa are two separate matters.

item.title: Your Baby Was Born in Korea and Is Not Korean: Registration, Status, and the 90-Day Clock
item.description: A child born in Korea to foreign parents does not become Korean and cannot be entered in the Korean family register. A Korean attorney explains the 90-day status application, embassy registration, and what happens when a Korean father is involved.

item.title: The E-2 Teaching Visa in Korea: What It Ties You To and What Breaks It
item.description: An E-2 visa is tied to one employer, not to teaching. A Korean attorney explains workplace change permission, what counts as unauthorized activity, and what happens to your status when a hagwon contract falls apart.

item.title: A Summary Order in Korea: The Criminal Conviction You Get by Paying and Saying Nothing
item.description: A summary order imposes a criminal fine with no hearing, and becomes final in seven days if you do nothing. A Korean attorney explains what it really is, when to request a formal trial, and why paying it can cost a foreign resident their visa.

item.title: Deportation and Entry Ban in Korea: Your Options Before You're Removed
item.description: A deportation order and a departure order are not the same thing, and the difference decides how long you're banned from returning. A Korean attorney explains the process, the 7-day objection window, and what still works.

item.title: F-3 Dependent Visa in Korea: Bringing Your Spouse and Children
item.description: Not every visa lets you bring your family to Korea, and an F-3 dependent cannot legally work without separate permission. A Korean attorney explains who qualifies, what to file, and the mistakes that cost families their status.

item.title: Your Korean Bank Account Was Frozen: What a Payment Suspension Really Means
item.description: One fraud report from a stranger can freeze your entire Korean bank account and block you from opening new ones. A Korean attorney explains why it happens to innocent foreigners and how to get the suspension lifted.

item.title: Copyright and Trademark Infringement in Korea: A Guide for Foreign Businesses
item.description: Korea runs on a first-to-file trademark system, and copyright protection abroad doesn't register your brand here. A Korean attorney explains what foreign businesses and creators need to know.

item.title: Online Gambling in Korea Is Illegal — Even on Foreign Sites
item.description: Betting on an offshore sportsbook or overseas casino site from inside Korea is a criminal offense, regardless of where the site is licensed. A Korean attorney explains the law and the risks for foreigners.

item.title: Fired During Your Probation Period in Korea? What Employers Can (and Can't) Do
item.description: A probation period (수습기간) in Korea doesn't mean at-will firing. A Korean attorney explains what protections foreign workers keep during probation, and how to respond to a sudden dismissal.

item.title: E-9 Visa (비전문취업) in Korea: What Non-Professional Foreign Workers Need to Know
item.description: The Employment Permit System (고용허가제), the limited grounds for a workplace change (사업장 변경), the re-entry special case (재입국 특례), and what your departure insurance (출국만기보험) is actually worth.

item.title: Flat Tax Rate (단일세율) for Foreign Workers in Korea: Is the Election Actually Worth It?
item.description: How the flat tax rate (단일세율) election works, who it actually benefits compared to the progressive tax rate (누진세율), and the filing mistakes that cost refunds.

item.title: Accused of Fraud (사기죄) in Korea? When a Business Dispute Becomes a Criminal Case
item.description: What actually separates criminal fraud (사기죄) from an ordinary breach of contract, why business disputes get filed as criminal complaints, and how to respond to a summons.

item.title: Data Privacy (개인정보보호법) in Korea for Foreign Residents
item.description: Your rights when a company mishandles or leaks your personal data in Korea — breach notification duties, free mediation, and statutory damages without proving loss.

item.title: E-7 Visa (특정활동) in Korea: Requirements for Specialized Foreign Workers
item.description: Which jobs qualify for the E-7 visa, the employer sponsorship requirements, the points-based E-7-4 route, and what to verify before accepting an offer.

item.title: Insult (모욕죄) in Korea: When a Rude Comment Becomes a Crime
item.description: How insult (모욕죄) differs from defamation, the public-perception requirement, the six-month complaint deadline, and the visa risk of even a minor conviction.

item.title: Common-Law Marriage (사실혼) in Korea for Foreign Partners
item.description: What a foreign partner in a de facto marriage (사실혼) actually gets under Korean law, what they don't, and why registering the marriage still matters.

item.title: D-2 Student Visa Part-Time Work Permit (시간제 취업허가) in Korea
item.description: The one-semester waiting rule, hour caps tied to your Korean ability, off-limits jobs, and the immigration risk of working without a permit — explained for international students.

item.title: Gift Tax (증여세) in Korea for Foreign Residents
item.description: Who counts as a taxable recipient, the deduction traps foreign families fall into, and the 3-month filing deadline — gift tax in Korea explained for foreign residents.

item.title: F-4 Visa (재외동포) in Korea: Overseas Korean Status Explained
item.description: Near-permanent residency without a job sponsor, and a short list of jobs it still doesn't allow — the F-4 overseas Korean visa, eligibility and limits explained.

item.title: Writing a Valid Will (유언장) in Korea as a Foreign Resident
item.description: Five statutory will forms, strict formality rules, and the forced heirship (유류분) claims that can override what the will says — wills in Korea explained for foreign residents.

item.title: Workplace Bullying (직장 내 괴롭힘) in Korea: A Foreign Employee's Guide
item.description: Excessive scolding, isolation, impossible workloads — workplace bullying (직장 내 괴롭힘) is a legal violation in Korea. The mandatory investigation process and remedies, explained for foreign employees.

item.title: Apostille and Document Authentication (아포스티유) in Korea: Getting Papers Recognized Abroad
item.description: Which agency certifies which document, and why apostille doesn't work everywhere — document authentication in Korea explained for foreign residents.

item.title: Lease Renewal Right (계약갱신청구권) in Korea: What Tenants Can Actually Demand
item.description: One renewal, a 5% rent cap, and a short list of reasons a landlord can refuse — the lease renewal right explained for foreign tenants in Korea.

item.title: Unemployment Benefits (실업급여) in Korea: What Foreign Workers Need to Qualify
item.description: 180 days of Employment Insurance, an involuntary separation, and active job-seeking — the real eligibility test for 실업급여, explained for foreign workers.

item.title: Adopting a Child in Korea as a Foreigner: What the Family Court Actually Requires
item.description: Eligibility, the Family Court approval process, and the home study every applicant has to pass — adoption in Korea explained for foreign residents.

item.title: Freelancer or Employee? Korea's Platform Worker Rules and What They Mean for You
item.description: The person-providing-labor (노무제공자) category, insurance rights it triggers, and how misclassification disputes actually play out for gig and platform workers in Korea.

item.title: Changing Your Legal Name After Naturalizing in Korea: The Court Approval Nobody Mentions
item.description: Name change (개명) after naturalization runs through Family Court, not the district office counter. The standard judges apply, and why some petitions get denied.
